Chew
chōō
v. (to grind with the teeth; in the law, to chew the cud, the second mark of a clean beast)
Old English ceowan, to chew. The Hebrew idiom of Leviticus 11 is literally “to bring up the cud” — the beast returns the food to the mouth and works it again.

Biblical Definition

“Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you” (Lev 11:4). Moses repeats the law in Deuteronomy with the camel, the hare, and the coney named: “for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you” (Deu 14:7). To chew the cud is to bring the food up from the stomach and grind it again — the beast eats its meal twice, and slowly. The old expositors, from the fathers through the Puritans, took it as the natural emblem of meditation on the word: not the swift reading that swallows a chapter whole, but the returning to it, the working of it over until the sweetness is out. Psalm 1 says the blessed man's delight is in the law of the LORD, and in his law doth he meditate day and night; Joshua is told the book shall not depart out of his mouth. The camel is the warning attached: a beast may ruminate all day and still be unclean, because meditation without a separated walk is not obedience. Both marks, or neither.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to chew as to bite and grind with the teeth; to masticate; and figuratively, to ruminate in the thoughts; to meditate.

expand to see more

CHEW, v.t. To bite and grind with the teeth; to masticate, as food, to prepare it for deglutition and digestion.

2. To ruminate in the thoughts; to meditate; as, to chew revenge.

3. To champ; to bite, hold or roll about in the mouth; as, to chew tobacco.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:4 — "Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you."

Deu 14:7 — "Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you."

Psa 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Modern Corruption

Reading has replaced ruminating: a generation with more Bible text available than any before it consumes chapters at speed and works none of them over, and calls the volume devotion.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and no one disputes it. What has been lost is the practice the clean beast pictures. The believer of 1650 might own one Bible, hear two sermons, and turn a single verse over for a week; the believer of today can carry every translation ever made in one hand, and the ordinary result is not depth but speed. Chewing the cud is a slow, repetitive, unglamorous business. It is reading the same paragraph on Tuesday that was read on Monday, and finding what Monday missed; it is carrying one clause into the workday and returning to it at noon; it is the psalmist's day and night. Meditation in the biblical sense has nothing to do with emptying the mind, which is the eastern practice that has borrowed the English word; it is filling the mind with a text and working it. The principle to recover is Joshua 1:8, where the promise of prosperity and good success is attached not to reading the book but to meditating therein day and night, and then doing according to all that is written.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'alah gerah, to bring up the cud; gerah (H1625), the cud; Hebrew hagah (H1897), to murmur, to muse, to meditate — the word of Psalm 1:2.

expand to see more

Hebrew gerah (H1625) — the cud; literally that which is brought up again and ground a second time; Leviticus 11:3-7, Deuteronomy 14:6-8.

Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to mutter, to muse; the blessed man's meditation, spoken low and continually; Psalm 1:2, Joshua 1:8.

Hebrew siyach (H7878) — to ponder, to converse with oneself; the psalmist meditating in the night watches; Psalm 119:15, 63:6.

Usage

"“Because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof” — the camel, unclean for want of the second mark."

"“They chew the cud, but divide not the hoof” — the camel, the hare, and the coney together."

"“In his law doth he meditate day and night” — the practice the clean beast pictures."
